newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU has no plans to tax wheat export -source.
newsitem.headline: EU has no plans to tax wheat export -source.

text.p: The European Union has no immediate plans to tax wheat exports, a senior European grain source familiar with Commission policy said on Friday.

However its decision to halt a weekly tender for wheat exports on Thursday, several weeks earlier than usual, was a signal that the EU had reached its volume target for the year and that it wanted to calm down domestic prices, he said.

"There has been no talk of a tax and there has been no talk of stopping other grain exports," the source said, responding to speculation in some markets that the EU was ready to bring back a controversial export tax used last year to save low supplies.
Such a tax, if it were imposed, would apply to the EU's alternative daily bidding system for wheat, which remains open.
But the system is already effectively under the Commission's control because it can reject bids within three working days.
Even though French and U.S. prices have swung closer together following the rise in Chicago overnight, the EU wants to avoid sending further tremors through the market.
"We want to avoid anything which would make the market more nervous," the source said.

Traders have already begun offering previously issued EU export licences to each other at taxes instead of subsidies. They use an informal derivative market based on settling the difference between a licence's face value and the traded value.
But the source said there would be no point in taxing exports at the end of the season.

The EU will instead leave its daily export channel open for so-called nil value licences. These export documents, effectively blank, allow shippers to cover business 30 days ahead but without any guarantee against a possible tax before they are used.
However the EU could decide to clamp down even on this procedure if bids for the licences get out of hand.

Ahead of Thursday's decision, Brussels released an unusually large 407,000 tonnes with daily licences this week and is set to let out another 70,000 tonnes late on Friday. But it has not yet decided how to react to any further bids, the source said.
"I imagine the next step might be to close this door as well, but there hasn't been any decision," he said.
Nor has the EU decided when to start the next export campaign, with all eyes on the dry weather that is grilling the next crop.
Analysts say that even if the EU wanted to discourage the export of a single grain of wheat, using the tax weapon could be worse than leaving the daily system as it is now.

Licences carrying any value -- a subsidy, tax or even a value of zero -- can be held for over four months and their value is prefixed or guaranteed. If world prices really started boiling again, making taxes affordable, traders might leap on the idea that the EU was ready to let its volume target slip.

"Nil value is a signal that the EU is more or less out of the business. Anything else is a signal that prefixing is available, and that is the wrong signal for domestic prices," the European grain source said.
The EU has exported some 9.6 million tonnes of commercial wheat grain this season, sharply up from last year.
